[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! global allocator (`dlmalloc`) so `Vec` works inside `#![no_std]`.
[76](https://docs.rs#76)
[77](https://docs.rs#77)use proc_macro::TokenStream;
[78](https://docs.rs#78)use proc_macro2::TokenStream as TokenStream2;
[79](https://docs.rs#79)use quote::{format_ident, quote};
[80](https://docs.rs#80)use syn::{parse_macro_input, FnArg, ItemFn, Pat, PatType, ReturnType, Type};
[81](https://docs.rs#81)
[82](https://docs.rs#82)/// Wrap a function with the Pyde entry-point shim.
[83](https://docs.rs#83)///
[84](https://docs.rs#84)/// See the crate-level docs for the expansion shape.
[85](https://docs.rs#85)#[proc_macro_attribute]
[86](https://docs.rs#86)pub fn entry(attr: TokenStream, item: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
[87](https://docs.rs#87)    if !attr.is_empty() {
[88](https://docs.rs#88)        // Attributes belong in otigen.toml. Reject here with a
[89](https://docs.rs#89)        // clear pointer instead of silently accepting + ignoring,
[90](https://docs.rs#90)        // which would create a Rust-says-X-but-ABI-says-Y
[91](https://docs.rs#91)        // divergence footgun.
[92](https://docs.rs#92)        let attr2: TokenStream2 = attr.into();
[93](https://docs.rs#93)        return syn::Error::new_spanned(
[94](https://docs.rs#94)            attr2,
[95](https://docs.rs#95)            "#[pyde::entry] takes no arguments. Function attributes \
[96](https://docs.rs#96)             (`view`, `payable`, `reentrant`, `constructor`, `fallback`, \
[97](https://docs.rs#97)             `receive`, `sponsored`) belong in `otigen.toml` under the \
[98](https://docs.rs#98)             matching `[functions.<name>] attributes = [...]` block. The \
[99](https://docs.rs#99)             chain reads them from the deployed pyde.abi section; \
[100](https://docs.rs#100)             duplicating them on the macro would create two sources of \
[101](https://docs.rs#101)             truth that could silently diverge.",
[102](https://docs.rs#102)        )
[103](https://docs.rs#103)        .to_compile_error()
[104](https://docs.rs#104)        .into();
[105](https://docs.rs#105)    }
[106](https://docs.rs#106)
[107](https://docs.rs#107)    let input = parse_macro_input!(item as ItemFn);
[108](https://docs.rs#108)    match expand_entry(input) {
[109](https://docs.rs#109)        Ok(ts) => ts.into(),
[110](https://docs.rs#110)        Err(e) => e.to_compile_error().into(),
[111](https://docs.rs#111)    }
[112](https://docs.rs#112)}
[113](https://docs.rs#113)
[114](https://docs.rs#114)fn expand_entry(input: ItemFn) -> Result<TokenStream2, syn::Error> {
[115](https://docs.rs#115)    let user_fn_name = input.sig.ident.clone();
[116](https://docs.rs#116)    let user_fn_vis = input.vis.clone();
[117](https://docs.rs#117)    let user_fn_attrs = input.attrs.clone();
[118](https://docs.rs#118)
[119](https://docs.rs#119)    // Pyde entry points are `() -> ()` at the WASM boundary. We reject
[120](https://docs.rs#120)    // any `async`, generic, or `unsafe` signatures upfront — none of
[121](https://docs.rs#121)    // them have honest semantics under the chain's dispatch convention.
[122](https://docs.rs#122)    if let Some(asyncness) = input.sig.asyncness {
[123](https://docs.rs#123)        return Err(syn::Error::new_spanned(
[124](https://docs.rs#124)            asyncness,
[125](https://docs.rs#125)            "#[pyde::entry] cannot be applied to async functions — Pyde entry points run \
[126](https://docs.rs#126)             synchronously inside the WASM call frame",
[127](https://docs.rs#127)        ));
[128](https://docs.rs#128)    }
[129](https://docs.rs#129)    if !input.sig.generics.params.is_empty() {
[130](https://docs.rs#130)        return Err(syn::Error::new_spanned(
[131](https://docs.rs#131)            &input.sig.generics,
[132](https://docs.rs#132)            "#[pyde::entry] cannot be applied to generic functions — entry points must be \
[133](https://docs.rs#133)             monomorphized at the WASM boundary",
[134](https://docs.rs#134)        ));
[135](https://docs.rs#135)    }
[136](https://docs.rs#136)    if let Some(unsafety) = input.sig.unsafety {
[137](https://docs.rs#137)        return Err(syn::Error::new_spanned(
[138](https://docs.rs#138)            unsafety,
[139](https://docs.rs#139)            "#[pyde::entry] cannot be applied to `unsafe fn` — the host invokes entry points \
[140](https://docs.rs#140)             from outside the contract, where `unsafe` carries no useful meaning",
[141](https://docs.rs#141)        ));
[142](https://docs.rs#142)    }
[143](https://docs.rs#143)    for arg in &input.sig.inputs {
[144](https://docs.rs#144)        if let FnArg::Receiver(rcv) = arg {
[145](https://docs.rs#145)            return Err(syn::Error::new_spanned(
[146](https://docs.rs#146)                rcv,
[147](https://docs.rs#147)                "#[pyde::entry] cannot be applied to methods (functions with `self`/`&self`/\
[148](https://docs.rs#148)                 `&mut self`) — entry points are free functions",
[149](https://docs.rs#149)            ));
[150](https://docs.rs#150)        }
[151](https://docs.rs#151)    }
[152](https://docs.rs#152)
[153](https://docs.rs#153)    let inner_ident = format_ident!("__pyde_entry_{}_inner", user_fn_name);
[154](https://docs.rs#154)
[155](https://docs.rs#155)    // Extract typed parameters as a (binding, type) pair list.
[156](https://docs.rs#156)    let typed_args: Vec<(Pat, Type)> = input
[157](https://docs.rs#157)        .sig
[158](https://docs.rs#158)        .inputs
[159](https://docs.rs#159)        .iter()
[160](https://docs.rs#160)        .filter_map(|a| match a {
[161](https://docs.rs#161)            FnArg::Typed(PatType { pat, ty, .. }) => Some(((**pat).clone(), (**ty).clone())),
[162](https://docs.rs#162)            FnArg::Receiver(_) => None,
[163](https://docs.rs#163)        })
[164](https://docs.rs#164)        .collect();
[165](https://docs.rs#165)
[166](https://docs.rs#166)    let arg_bindings: Vec<Pat> = typed_args.iter().map(|(p, _)| p.clone()).collect();
[167](https://docs.rs#167)    let arg_types: Vec<Type> = typed_args.iter().map(|(_, t)| t.clone()).collect();
[168](https://docs.rs#168)    let inner_call_args: Vec<Pat> = arg_bindings.clone();
[169](https://docs.rs#169)
[170](https://docs.rs#170)    // Decode block: empty when the function takes no args.
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    //
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    // Host ABI: `calldata_copy(out_ptr, out_len_ptr) -> i32`. The
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    // contract writes the buffer's max-bytes (LE u32) to
[174](https://docs.rs#174)    // `out_len_ptr`; the host caps at that limit, copies bytes to
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    // `out_ptr`, and writes the actual length back to `out_len_ptr`.
[176](https://docs.rs#176)    // (HOST_FN_ABI_SPEC §7.4.)
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    let calldata_load: TokenStream2 = quote! {
[178](https://docs.rs#178)        let __pyde_size = unsafe { ::pyde_host::raw::calldata_size() } as usize;
[179](https://docs.rs#179)        let mut __pyde_buf = ::alloc::vec![0u8; __pyde_size];
[180](https://docs.rs#180)        if __pyde_size > 0 {
[181](https://docs.rs#181)            let mut __pyde_limit: [u8; 4] = (__pyde_size as u32).to_le_bytes();
[182](https://docs.rs#182)            unsafe {
[183](https://docs.rs#183)                ::pyde_host::raw::calldata_copy(
[184](https://docs.rs#184)                    __pyde_buf.as_mut_ptr(),
[185](https://docs.rs#185)                    __pyde_limit.as_mut_ptr(),
[186](https://docs.rs#186)                );
[187](https://docs.rs#187)            }
[188](https://docs.rs#188)        }
[189](https://docs.rs#189)    };
[190](https://docs.rs#190)    let decode_block: TokenStream2 = if typed_args.is_empty() {
[191](https://docs.rs#191)        quote! {}
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    } else if typed_args.len() == 1 {
[193](https://docs.rs#193)        let pat = &arg_bindings[0];
[194](https://docs.rs#194)        let ty = &arg_types[0];
[195](https://docs.rs#195)        quote! {
[196](https://docs.rs#196)            #calldata_load
[197](https://docs.rs#197)            let #pat: #ty =
[198](https://docs.rs#198)                <#ty as ::borsh::BorshDeserialize>::try_from_slice(&__pyde_buf)
[199](https://docs.rs#199)                    .expect("calldata decode");
[200](https://docs.rs#200)        }
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    } else {
[202](https://docs.rs#202)        quote! {
[203](https://docs.rs#203)            #calldata_load
[204](https://docs.rs#204)            let ( #( #arg_bindings ),* ): ( #( #arg_types ),* ) =
[205](https://docs.rs#205)                <( #( #arg_types ),* ) as ::borsh::BorshDeserialize>::try_from_slice(
[206](https://docs.rs#206)                    &__pyde_buf,
[207](https://docs.rs#207)                )
[208](https://docs.rs#208)                .expect("calldata decode");
[209](https://docs.rs#209)        }
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    };
[211](https://docs.rs#211)
[212](https://docs.rs#212)    // Inner-call + return-wrap. Unit returns don't go through
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    // `pyde::return`; non-unit returns get borsh-encoded.
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    let returns_unit = matches!(input.sig.output, ReturnType::Default)
[215](https://docs.rs#215)        || matches!(&input.sig.output, ReturnType::Type(_, ty) if is_unit(ty));
[216](https://docs.rs#216)
[217](https://docs.rs#217)    let invocation: TokenStream2 = if returns_unit {
[218](https://docs.rs#218)        quote! {
[219](https://docs.rs#219)            #inner_ident( #( #inner_call_args ),* );
[220](https://docs.rs#220)        }
[221](https://docs.rs#221)    } else {
[222](https://docs.rs#222)        quote! {
[223](https://docs.rs#223)            let __pyde_result = #inner_ident( #( #inner_call_args ),* );
[224](https://docs.rs#224)            let __pyde_bytes =
[225](https://docs.rs#225)                ::borsh::to_vec(&__pyde_result).expect("encode return");
[226](https://docs.rs#226)            unsafe {
[227](https://docs.rs#227)                ::pyde_host::raw::pyde_return(
[228](https://docs.rs#228)                    __pyde_bytes.as_ptr(),
[229](https://docs.rs#229)                    __pyde_bytes.len() as i32,
[230](https://docs.rs#230)                )
[231](https://docs.rs#231)            };
[232](https://docs.rs#232)        }
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    };
[234](https://docs.rs#234)
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    // Rename the user's function (signature + body intact) so the
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    // shim can call it. Strip the original `#[no_mangle]` / `pub
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    // extern "C"` if the author left them on — the shim owns those.
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    let mut inner_fn = input.clone();
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    inner_fn.sig.ident = inner_ident.clone();
[240](https://docs.rs#240)    inner_fn.vis = syn::Visibility::Inherited;
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    inner_fn.attrs.clear();
[242](https://docs.rs#242)
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    // ── Signature record for toolchain cross-checking ───────────
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    //
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    // Emit the TRUE Rust signature into a `pyde.sig.v1` custom
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    // section so `otigen build` can verify the manifest's declared
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    // `[functions.<fn>] inputs / outputs` against the code instead of
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    // trusting hand-written metadata. One length-prefixed text record
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    // per entry — the linker concatenates every entry's static into a
[250](https://docs.rs#250)    // single custom section. Format:
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    //
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    //   <name>(<RustTy>,<RustTy>)->[RustTy];
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    //
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    // Types are the normalized token strings of the user's own
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    // annotations (whitespace stripped); the toolchain owns the
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    // Rust-type → manifest-token mapping. Tools that don't know the
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    // section ignore it; chains never see it (otigen strips nothing —
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    // it's ignored by the engine's import/export validation, which
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    // only inspects imports, exports, and `pyde.abi`).
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    let sig_record = {
[261](https://docs.rs#261)        let params = typed_args
[262](https://docs.rs#262)            .iter()
[263](https://docs.rs#263)            .map(|(_, ty)| normalize_type(ty))
[264](https://docs.rs#264)            .collect::<Vec<_>>()
[265](https://docs.rs#265)            .join(",");
[266](https://docs.rs#266)        let ret = match &input.sig.output {
[267](https://docs.rs#267)            ReturnType::Default => String::new(),
[268](https://docs.rs#268)            ReturnType::Type(_, ty) if is_unit(ty) => String::new(),
[269](https://docs.rs#269)            ReturnType::Type(_, ty) => normalize_type(ty),
[270](https://docs.rs#270)        };
[271](https://docs.rs#271)        format!("{user_fn_name}({params})->{ret};")
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    };
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    let sig_bytes = sig_record.as_bytes();
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    let sig_len = sig_bytes.len();
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    let sig_static = format_ident!("__PYDE_SIG_{}", user_fn_name);
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    let sig_byte_tokens = sig_bytes.iter().map(|b| quote! { #b });
[277](https://docs.rs#277)
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    Ok(quote! {
[279](https://docs.rs#279)        #[used]
[280](https://docs.rs#280)        #[link_section = "pyde.sig.v1"]
[281](https://docs.rs#281)        #[doc(hidden)]
[282](https://docs.rs#282)        static #sig_static: [u8; #sig_len] = [ #( #sig_byte_tokens ),* ];
[283](https://docs.rs#283)
[284](https://docs.rs#284)        #( #user_fn_attrs )*
[285](https://docs.rs#285)        #[no_mangle]
[286](https://docs.rs#286)        #user_fn_vis extern "C" fn #user_fn_name() {
[287](https://docs.rs#287)            #inner_fn
[288](https://docs.rs#288)
[289](https://docs.rs#289)            #decode_block
[290](https://docs.rs#290)            #invocation
[291](https://docs.rs#291)        }
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    })
[293](https://docs.rs#293)}
[294](https://docs.rs#294)
[295](https://docs.rs#295)/// Render a `syn::Type` as its user-written token string with all
[296](https://docs.rs#296)/// whitespace stripped — `Vec < u64 >` → `Vec<u64>` — so the record
[297](https://docs.rs#297)/// format is stable regardless of formatting.
[298](https://docs.rs#298)fn normalize_type(ty: &Type) -> String {
[299](https://docs.rs#299)    let raw = quote::quote!(#ty).to_string();

[301](https://docs.rs#301)}

# aes_gcm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/aes-gcm/^0.10/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rustcrypto-aes-gcm)RustCrypto: AES-GCM

Pure Rust implementation of the AES-GCM
[Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authenticated_encryption) cipher.

[§](https://docs.rs#security-notes)Security Notes

This crate has received one [security audit by NCC Group](https://research.nccgroup.com/2020/02/26/public-report-rustcrypto-aes-gcm-and-chacha20poly1305-implementation-review/), with no significant
findings. We would like to thank [MobileCoin](https://www.mobilecoin.com/) for funding the audit.

All implementations contained in the crate are designed to execute in constant time, either by relying on hardware intrinsics (i.e. AES-NI and CLMUL on x86/x86_64), or using a portable implementation which is only constant time on processors which implement constant-time multiplication.

It is not suitable for use on processors with a variable-time multiplication operation (e.g. short circuit on multiply-by-zero / multiply-by-one, such as certain 32-bit PowerPC CPUs and some non-ARM microcontrollers).

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

Licensed under either of:

at your option.

[§](https://docs.rs#contribution)Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Simple usage (allocating, no associated data):

```
use aes_gcm::{
    aead::{Aead, AeadCore, KeyInit, OsRng},
    Aes256Gcm, Nonce, Key // Or `Aes128Gcm`
};
// The encryption key can be generated randomly:
let key = Aes256Gcm::generate_key(OsRng);
// Transformed from a byte array:
let key: &[u8; 32] = &[42; 32];
let key: &Key<Aes256Gcm> = key.into();
// Note that you can get byte array from slice using the `TryInto` trait:
let key: &[u8] = &[42; 32];
let key: [u8; 32] = key.try_into()?;
// Alternatively, the key can be transformed directly from a byte slice
// (panicks on length mismatch):
let key = Key::<Aes256Gcm>::from_slice(key);
let cipher = Aes256Gcm::new(&key);
let nonce = Aes256Gcm::generate_nonce(&mut OsRng); // 96-bits; unique per message
let ciphertext = cipher.encrypt(&nonce, b"plaintext message".as_ref())?;
let plaintext = cipher.decrypt(&nonce, ciphertext.as_ref())?;
assert_eq!(&plaintext, b"plaintext message");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#in-place-usage-eliminates-alloc-requirement)In-place Usage (eliminates `alloc` requirement)

This crate has an optional `alloc` feature which can be disabled in e.g.
microcontroller environments that don’t have a heap.

The [ AeadInPlace::encrypt_in_place](https://docs.rs/trait.AeadInPlace.html#method.encrypt_in_place) and

[methods accept any type that impls the](https://docs.rs/trait.AeadInPlace.html#method.decrypt_in_place)

`AeadInPlace::decrypt_in_place`[trait which contains the plaintext for encryption or ciphertext for decryption.](https://docs.rs/aead/0.5.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aead/trait.Buffer.html)

`aead::Buffer`Note that if you enable the `heapless` feature of this crate,
you will receive an impl of [ aead::Buffer](https://docs.rs/aead/0.5.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aead/trait.Buffer.html) for

`heapless::Vec`
(re-exported from the [crate as](https://docs.rs/aead/0.5.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aead/index.html)

`aead`[), which can then be passed as the](https://docs.rs/heapless/0.7.17/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/heapless/vec/struct.Vec.html)

`aead::heapless::Vec``buffer` parameter to the in-place encrypt
and decrypt methods:```
use aes_gcm::{
    aead::{AeadCore, AeadInPlace, KeyInit, OsRng, heapless::Vec},
    Aes256Gcm, Nonce, // Or `Aes128Gcm`
};
let key = Aes256Gcm::generate_key(&mut OsRng);
let cipher = Aes256Gcm::new(&key);
let nonce = Aes256Gcm::generate_nonce(&mut OsRng); // 96-bits; unique per message
let mut buffer: Vec<u8, 128> = Vec::new(); // Note: buffer needs 16-bytes overhead for auth tag
buffer.extend_from_slice(b"plaintext message");
// Encrypt `buffer` in-place, replacing the plaintext contents with ciphertext
cipher.encrypt_in_place(&nonce, b"", &mut buffer)?;
// `buffer` now contains the message ciphertext
assert_ne!(&buffer, b"plaintext message");
// Decrypt `buffer` in-place, replacing its ciphertext context with the original plaintext
cipher.decrypt_in_place(&nonce, b"", &mut buffer)?;
assert_eq!(&buffer, b"plaintext message");
```
Similarly, enabling the `arrayvec` feature of this crate will provide an impl of
[ aead::Buffer](https://docs.rs/aead/0.5.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aead/trait.Buffer.html) for

`arrayvec::ArrayVec` (re-exported from the [crate as](https://docs.rs/aead/0.5.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aead/index.html)

`aead`[).](https://docs.rs/arrayvec/0.7.6/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/arrayvec/arrayvec/struct.ArrayVec.html)

`aead::arrayvec::ArrayVec`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

# hmac - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hmac/^0.12/

## Expand description

Generic implementation of Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC).

To use it you will need a cryptographic hash function implementation which
implements the [ digest](https://docs.rs/digest) crate traits. You can find compatible crates
(e.g.

[) in the](https://docs.rs/sha2)

`sha2`[repository.](https://github.com/RustCrypto/hashes)

`RustCrypto/hashes`This crate provides two HMAC implementation [ Hmac](https://docs.rs/type.Hmac.html) and

[. The first one is a buffered wrapper around block-level](https://docs.rs/struct.SimpleHmac.html)

`SimpleHmac`[. Internally it uses efficient state representation, but works only with hash functions which expose block-level API and consume blocks eagerly (e.g. it will not work with the BLAKE2 family of hash functions). On the other hand,](https://docs.rs/struct.HmacCore.html)

`HmacCore`[is a bit less efficient memory-wise, but works with all hash functions which implement the](https://docs.rs/struct.SimpleHmac.html)

`SimpleHmac`[trait.](https://docs.rs/digest)

`Digest`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Let us demonstrate how to use HMAC using the SHA-256 hash function.

In the following examples [ Hmac](https://docs.rs/type.Hmac.html) is interchangeable with

[.](https://docs.rs/struct.SimpleHmac.html)

`SimpleHmac`To get authentication code:

```
use sha2::Sha256;
use hmac::{Hmac, Mac};
use hex_literal::hex;
// Create alias for HMAC-SHA256
type HmacSha256 = Hmac<Sha256>;
let mut mac = HmacSha256::new_from_slice(b"my secret and secure key")
    .expect("HMAC can take key of any size");
mac.update(b"input message");
// `result` has type `CtOutput` which is a thin wrapper around array of
// bytes for providing constant time equality check
let result = mac.finalize();
// To get underlying array use `into_bytes`, but be careful, since
// incorrect use of the code value may permit timing attacks which defeats
// the security provided by the `CtOutput`
let code_bytes = result.into_bytes();
let expected = hex!("
    97d2a569059bbcd8ead4444ff99071f4
    c01d005bcefe0d3567e1be628e5fdcd9
");
assert_eq!(code_bytes[..], expected[..]);
```
To verify the message:

```
let mut mac = HmacSha256::new_from_slice(b"my secret and secure key")
    .expect("HMAC can take key of any size");
mac.update(b"input message");
let code_bytes = hex!("
    97d2a569059bbcd8ead4444ff99071f4
    c01d005bcefe0d3567e1be628e5fdcd9
");
// `verify_slice` will return `Ok(())` if code is correct, `Err(MacError)` otherwise
mac.verify_slice(&code_bytes[..]).unwrap();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#block-and-input-sizes)Block and input sizes

Usually it is assumed that block size is larger than output size. Due to the generic nature of the implementation, this edge case must be handled as well to remove potential panic. This is done by truncating hash output to the hash block size if needed.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [digest](https://docs.rs/digest/0.10.7/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/digest/index.html);

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Hmac](https://docs.rs/struct.HmacCore.html)- Core
- Generic core HMAC instance, which operates over blocks.
- [Simple](https://docs.rs/struct.SimpleHmac.html)- Hmac
- Simplified HMAC instance able to operate over hash functions which do not expose block-level API and hash functions which process blocks lazily (e.g. BLAKE2).

- Convenience wrapper trait covering functionality of Message Authentication algorithms.

# k256 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/k256/^0.13/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rustcrypto-secp256k1-k-256-elliptic-curve)[RustCrypto](https://github.com/RustCrypto/): secp256k1 (K-256) elliptic curve

[secp256k1](https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Secp256k1) (a.k.a. K-256) elliptic curve library written in pure Rust with
support for [ECDSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_Curve_Digital_Signature_Algorithm) signing/verification/public-key recovery, Taproot
[Schnorr signatures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schnorr_signature) as defined in BIP340, Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH),
and general-purpose secp256k1 elliptic curve group operations which can be used
to implement arbitrary group-based protocols.

Uses traits and base types from the [ elliptic-curve](https://github.com/RustCrypto/traits/tree/master/elliptic-curve) crate.

Optionally includes a secp256k1 [ arithmetic](https://docs.rs/k256/latest/k256/arithmetic/index.html) feature providing scalar and
point types (projective/affine) with support for constant-time scalar
multiplication. Additionally, implements traits from the

[crate which can be used to generically construct group-based protocols.](https://github.com/zkcrypto/group)

`group`[§](https://docs.rs#security-notes)Security Notes

This crate has been [audited by NCC Group](https://research.nccgroup.com/2023/08/30/public-report-entropy-rust-cryptography-review/), which found a high severity issue
in the ECDSA/secp256k1 implementation and another high severity issue in the
Schnorr/secp256k1 signature implementation, both of which have since been
corrected. We would like to thank [Entropy](https://entropy.xyz/) for funding the audit.

This crate has been designed with the goal of ensuring that secret-dependent
secp256k1 operations are performed in constant time (using the `subtle` crate
and constant-time formulas). However, it is not suitable for use on processors
with a variable-time multiplication operation (e.g. short circuit on
multiply-by-zero / multiply-by-one, such as certain 32-bit PowerPC CPUs and
some non-ARM microcontrollers).

USE AT YOUR OWN RISK!

[§](https://docs.rs#supported-algorithms)Supported Algorithms

- [Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic-curve_Diffie-Hellman): gated under the- `ecdh`feature. Note that this is technically ephemeral secp256k1 Diffie-Hellman (a.k.a. ECDHE)
- [Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_Curve_Digital_Signature_Algorithm): gated under the- `ecdsa`feature. Support for ECDSA/secp256k1 signing and verification, applying- [low-S normalization (BIP 0062)](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0062.mediawiki)as used in consensus-critical applications, and additionally supports secp256k1 public-key recovery from ECDSA signatures (as used by e.g. Ethereum)
- Taproot [Schnorr signatures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schnorr_signature)(as defined in[BIP0340](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0340.mediawiki)): next-generation signature algorithm based on group operations enabling elegant higher-level constructions like multisignatures.

[§](https://docs.rs#about-secp256k1-k-256)About secp256k1 (K-256)

[secp256k1](https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Secp256k1) is a Koblitz curve commonly used in cryptocurrency applications.
The “K-256” name follows NIST notation where P = prime fields,
B = binary fields, and K = Koblitz curves.

The curve is specified as `secp256k1` by Certicom’s SECG in
“SEC 2: Recommended Elliptic Curve Domain Parameters”:

secp256k1 is primarily notable for usage in Bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies,
particularly in conjunction with the
[Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_Curve_Digital_Signature_Algorithm).
Owing to its wide deployment in these applications, secp256k1 is one of the
most popular and commonly used elliptic curves.

# p256 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/p256/^0.13/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rustcrypto-nist-p-256-secp256r1-elliptic-curve)[RustCrypto](https://github.com/rustcrypto/): NIST P-256 (secp256r1) elliptic curve

Pure Rust implementation of the NIST P-256 (a.k.a. secp256r1, prime256v1)
elliptic curve with support for ECDH, ECDSA signing/verification, and general
purpose curve arithmetic support implemented in terms of traits from the
[ elliptic-curve](https://github.com/RustCrypto/traits/tree/master/elliptic-curve) crate.

[§](https://docs.rs#-security-warning)⚠️ Security Warning

The elliptic curve arithmetic contained in this crate has never been independently audited!

This crate has been designed with the goal of ensuring that secret-dependent
operations are performed in constant time (using the `subtle` crate and
constant-time formulas). However, it has not been thoroughly assessed to ensure
that generated assembly is constant time on common CPU architectures.

USE AT YOUR OWN RISK!

[§](https://docs.rs#supported-algorithms)Supported Algorithms

- [Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_Curve_Digital_Signature_Algorithm): gated under the- `ecdsa`feature.

[§](https://docs.rs#about-nist-p-256)About NIST P-256

NIST P-256 is a Weierstrass curve specified in [SP 800-186](https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-186/final):
Recommendations for Discrete Logarithm-based Cryptography:
Elliptic Curve Domain Parameters.

Also known as prime256v1 (ANSI X9.62) and secp256r1 (SECG), it’s included in the US National Security Agency’s “Suite B” and is widely used in protocols like TLS and the associated X.509 PKI.

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.8/

## Expand description

Utilities for random number generation

Rand provides utilities to generate random numbers, to convert them to useful types and distributions, and some randomness-related algorithms.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

To get you started quickly, the easiest and highest-level way to get
a random value is to use [ random()](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html); alternatively you can use

[. The](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html)

`thread_rng()`[trait provides a useful API on all RNGs, while the](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[and](https://docs.rs/distributions/index.html)

`distributions`[modules provide further functionality on top of RNGs.](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)

`seq````
use rand::prelude::*;
if rand::random() { // generates a boolean
    // Try printing a random unicode code point (probably a bad idea)!
    println!("char: {}", rand::random::<char>());
}
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
let y: f64 = rng.gen(); // generates a float between 0 and 1
let mut nums: Vec<i32> = (1..100).collect();
nums.shuffle(&mut rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-book)The Book

For the user guide and further documentation, please read
[The Rust Rand Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

[RustCrypto](https://github.com/RustCrypto/): RSA

A portable RSA implementation in pure Rust.

## Example

```
use ;
let mut rng = thread_rng; // rand@0.8
let bits = 2048;
let priv_key = new.expect;
let pub_key = from;
// Encrypt
let data = b"hello world";
let enc_data = pub_key.encrypt.expect;
assert_ne!;
// Decrypt
let dec_data = priv_key.decrypt.expect;
assert_eq!;
```

Note:If you encounter unusually slow key generation time while using`RsaPrivateKey::new`you can try to compile in release mode or add the following to your`Cargo.toml`. Key generation is much faster when building with higher optimization levels, but this will increase the compile time a bit.`[] = 3`If you don't want to turn on optimizations for all dependencies, you can only optimize the

`num-bigint-dig`dependency. This should give most of the speedups.`[] = 3`

## ⚠️Security Warning

This crate has received one [security audit by Include Security](https://www.opentech.fund/results/security-safety-audits/deltachat/), with
only one minor finding which has since been addressed.

See the [open security issues](https://github.com/RustCrypto/RSA/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3Asecurity) on our issue tracker for other known problems.

~~Notably the implementation of ~~ This crate is vulnerable to the [modular exponentiation is not constant time](https://github.com/RustCrypto/RSA/issues/19),
but timing variability is masked using [random blinding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blinding_(cryptography)), a commonly used
technique.[Marvin Attack](https://people.redhat.com/~hkario/marvin/) which could enable
private key recovery by a network attacker (see [RUSTSEC-2023-0071](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2023-0071.html)).

You can follow our work on mitigating this issue in [#390](https://github.com/RustCrypto/RSA/issues/390).

# sha1 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sha1/^0.10/

## Expand description

Pure Rust implementation of the [SHA-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SHA-1) cryptographic hash algorithm
with optional hardware-specific optimizations.

[§](https://docs.rs#-warning-cryptographically-broken-)🚨 Warning: Cryptographically Broken! 🚨

The SHA-1 hash function should be considered cryptographically broken and
unsuitable for further use in any security critical capacity, as it is
[practically vulnerable to chosen-prefix collisions](https://sha-mbles.github.io/).

We provide this crate for legacy interoperability purposes only.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

```
use hex_literal::hex;
use sha1::{Sha1, Digest};
// create a Sha1 object
let mut hasher = Sha1::new();
// process input message
hasher.update(b"hello world");
// acquire hash digest in the form of GenericArray,
// which in this case is equivalent to [u8; 20]
let result = hasher.finalize();
assert_eq!(result[..], hex!("2aae6c35c94fcfb415dbe95f408b9ce91ee846ed"));
```
Also see [RustCrypto/hashes](https://github.com/RustCrypto/hashes) readme.

[§](https://docs.rs#note-for-users-of-sha1-v06)Note for users of `sha1 v0.6`

This crate has been transferred to the RustCrypto organization and uses
implementation previously published as the `sha-1` crate. The previous
zero dependencies version is now published as the [ sha1_smol](https://github.com/mitsuhiko/sha1-smol/) crate.

# signature - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/signature/^2/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#rustcrypto-digital-signature-algorithms)[RustCrypto](https://github.com/RustCrypto/): Digital Signature Algorithms

This crate contains traits which provide generic, object-safe APIs for
generating and verifying [digital signatures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_signature).

Used by the [ dsa](https://github.com/RustCrypto/signatures/tree/master/dsa),

[,](https://github.com/RustCrypto/signatures/tree/master/ecdsa)

`ecdsa`[, and](https://github.com/RustCrypto/signatures/tree/master/ed25519)

`ed25519`[crates maintained by the](https://github.com/RustCrypto/RSA)

`rsa`[RustCrypto](https://github.com/RustCrypto/)organization, as well as

[.](https://github.com/dalek-cryptography/ed25519-dalek)

`ed25519-dalek`[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version)Minimum Supported Rust Version

Rust **1.60** or higher.

Minimum supported Rust version can be changed in the future, but it will be done with a minor version bump.

[§](https://docs.rs#semver-policy)SemVer Policy

- All on-by-default features of this library are covered by SemVer
- MSRV is considered exempt from SemVer as noted above
- The `derive`feature is stable and covered by SemVer
- The off-by-default features `digest`and`rand_core`are unstable features which are also considered exempt from SemVer as they correspond to pre-1.0 crates which are still subject to changes. Breaking changes to these features will, like MSRV, be done with a minor version bump.

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

Licensed under either of

at your option.

[§](https://docs.rs#contribution)Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

This crate provides a common set of traits for signing and verifying digital signatures intended to be implemented by libraries which produce or contain implementations of digital signature algorithms, and used by libraries which want to produce or verify digital signatures while generically supporting any compatible backend.

[§](https://docs.rs#goals)Goals

The traits provided by this crate were designed with the following goals in mind:

- Provide an easy-to-use, misuse resistant API optimized for consumers (as opposed to implementers) of its traits.
- Support common type-safe wrappers around “bag-of-bytes” representations which can be directly parsed from or written to the “wire”.
- Expose a trait/object-safe API where signers/verifiers spanning multiple homogeneous provider implementations can be seamlessly leveraged together in the same logical “keyring” so long as they operate on the same underlying signature type.
- Allow one provider type to potentially implement support (including being generic over) several signature types.
- Keep signature algorithm customizations / “knobs” out-of-band from the signing/verification APIs, ideally pushing such concerns into the type system so that algorithm mismatches are caught as type errors.
- Opaque error type which minimizes information leaked from cryptographic
failures, as “rich” error types in these scenarios are often a source
of sidechannel information for attackers (e.g. [BB’06](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Bleichenbacher))

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation)Implementation

To accomplish the above goals, the [ Signer](https://docs.rs/trait.Signer.html) and

[traits provided by this are generic over a signature value, and use generic parameters rather than associated types. Notably, they use such a parameter for the return value, allowing it to be inferred by the type checker based on the desired signature type.](https://docs.rs/trait.Verifier.html)

`Verifier`[§](https://docs.rs#alternatives-considered)Alternatives considered

This crate is based on many years of exploration of how to encapsulate digital signature systems in the most flexible, developer-friendly way. During that time many design alternatives were explored, tradeoffs compared, and ultimately the provided API was selected.

The tradeoffs made in this API have all been to improve simplicity,
ergonomics, type safety, and flexibility for *consumers* of the traits.
At times, this has come at a cost to implementers. Below are some concerns
we are cognizant of which were considered in the design of the API:

- “Bag-of-bytes” serialization precludes signature providers from using their own internal representation of a signature, which can be helpful for many reasons (e.g. advanced signature system features like batch verification).
- Associated types, rather than generic parameters of traits, could allow more customization of the types used by a particular signature system, e.g. using custom error types.

It may still make sense to continue to explore the above tradeoffs, but
with a *new* set of traits which are intended to be implementor-friendly,
rather than consumer friendly. The existing [ Signer](https://docs.rs/trait.Signer.html) and

[traits could have blanket impls for the “provider-friendly” traits. However, as noted above this is a design space easily explored after stabilizing the consumer-oriented traits, and thus we consider these more important.](https://docs.rs/trait.Verifier.html)

`Verifier`That said, below are some caveats of trying to design such traits, and why we haven’t actively pursued them:

- Generics in the return position are already used to select which trait impl to use, i.e. for a particular signature algorithm/system. Avoiding a unified, concrete signature type adds another dimension to complexity and compiler errors, and in our experience makes them unsuitable for this sort of API. We believe such an API is the natural one for signature systems, reflecting the natural way they are written absent a trait.
- Associated types preclude multiple implementations of the same trait. These parameters are common in signature systems, notably ones which support different serializations of a signature (e.g. raw vs ASN.1).
- Digital signatures are almost always larger than the present 32-entry
trait impl limitation on array types, which complicates bounds
for these types (particularly things like `From`or`Borrow`bounds).

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable features

Despite being post-1.0, this crate includes off-by-default unstable optional features, each of which depends on a pre-1.0 crate.

These features are considered exempt from SemVer. See the
[SemVer policy](https://docs.rs#semver-policy) above for more information.

The following unstable features are presently supported:

- `digest`: enables the- `DigestSigner`- `DigestVerifier`- `Digest`- `digest`- [Fiat-Shamir heuristic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiat%E2%80%93Shamir_heuristic)which compute a random challenge value to sign by computing a cryptographically secure digest of the input message.
- `rand_core`: enables the- `RandomizedSigner`

NOTE: the [ async-signature](https://docs.rs/async-signature) crate contains experimental

`async` support
for [and](https://docs.rs/trait.Signer.html)

`Signer`[.](https://docs.rs/trait.DigestSigner.html)

# fakecloud_kms::hook - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fakecloud-kms/0.31.0/fakecloud_kms/hook/index.html

## Expand description

Cross-service KMS hook.

Services that accept a `KmsKeyId` (Secrets Manager, SSM
`SecureString`, S3 SSE-KMS, SQS, SNS, DynamoDB) call into this
module so that:

- The supplied key is resolved (alias `aws/<service>`and bare aliases included), auto-provisioning AWS-managed keys on first use to match real AWS.
- Each call is recorded in `KmsUsageState``/_fakecloud/kms/usage`that the right service triggered the right operation on the right key.
- The returned ciphertext is a real envelope decryptable by the
public KMS `Decrypt`API (uses the same`fakecloud-kms:`envelope as the existing service-side encrypt path).

Encryption context, key policy enforcement, and KMS-managed key rotation come in follow-up PRs.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [KmsService](https://docs.rs/struct.KmsServiceHook.html)- Hook
- Hook used by service crates that need to call KMS for encryption / decryption without going through the AWS-shaped HTTP layer.
- [KmsUsage](https://docs.rs/struct.KmsUsageRecord.html)- Record
- One recorded KMS hook call. Returned by the introspection endpoint
so test code can assert `kms:GenerateDataKey`/`kms:Decrypt`ran on the expected key + service principal.
- [KmsUsage](https://docs.rs/struct.KmsUsageState.html)- State

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_AWS_MANAGED_ALIASES.html)- AWS_ - MANAGED_ - ALIASES
- Canonical AWS-managed service aliases (`alias/aws/<service>`). Real AWS pre-creates these in every account/region, so`aws kms list-aliases`returns them on a brand-new account and`data.aws_kms_alias`resolves them. The Terraform acceptance tests for several services (e.g.`aws_dynamodb_table`encryption) read`alias/aws/<service>`via that data source, so they must be listable even before any KMS use.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [ensure_](https://docs.rs/fn.ensure_default_managed_aliases.html)- default_ - managed_ - aliases
- Idempotently provision every `DEFAULT_AWS_MANAGED_ALIASES``ListAliases`mirrors real AWS. Provisioning a missing alias also mints its backing AWS-managed key, matching the auto-provision-on-first-use path in [`resolve_or_provision`].

# fakecloud_kms::resource_policy - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fakecloud-kms/0.31.0/fakecloud_kms/resource_policy/index.html

## Expand description

KMS implementation of [ ResourcePolicyProvider](https://docs.rs/fakecloud-core/0.31.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/fakecloud_core/auth/trait.ResourcePolicyProvider.html).

Every KMS key carries a key policy (stored in [`KmsKey::policy`]).
`CreateKey` auto-generates a default policy granting `kms:*` to the
account root, matching AWS behavior. `PutKeyPolicy` / `GetKeyPolicy`
replace and read it. This provider is the read-side bridge into the
`fakecloud-core::auth::ResourcePolicyProvider` trait so the IAM
evaluator can combine key policies with identity policies.

---

Build a hook that persists the current KMS state when invoked, or
`None` in memory mode (no snapshot store). The CloudFormation provisioner
mutates `state` directly and uses this to write a CFN-provisioned
resource through to disk, the same way a direct mutating API call would.

# flate2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/flate2/^1/

## Expand description

A DEFLATE-based stream compression/decompression library

This library provides support for compression and decompression of DEFLATE-based streams:

- the DEFLATE format itself
- the zlib format
- gzip

These three formats are all closely related and largely only differ in their headers/footers. This crate has three types in each submodule for dealing with these three formats.

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation)Implementation

In addition to supporting three formats, this crate supports several different
backends, controlled through this crate’s *features flags*:

-
`default`, or`rust_backend`- this implementation currently uses the`miniz_oxide`crate which is a port of`miniz.c`to Rust. This feature does not require a C compiler, and only uses safe Rust code.Note that the `rust_backend`feature may at some point be switched to use`zlib-rs`, and that`miniz_oxide`should be used explicitly if this is not desired.
-
`zlib-rs`- this implementation utilizes the`zlib-rs`crate, a Rust rewrite of zlib. This backend is the fastest, at the cost of some`unsafe`Rust code.

Several backends implemented in C are also available. These are useful in case you are already using a specific C implementation and need the result of compression to be bit-identical. See the crate’s README for details on the available C backends.

The `zlib-rs` backend typically outperforms all the C implementations.

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

- `miniz_oxide`- *(enabled by default)*— This implementation uses only safe Rust code and doesn’t require a C compiler. It provides good performance for most use cases while being completely portable.
- `default`

[§](https://docs.rs#user-facing-backend-features)User-Facing Backend Features

Choose one of these features to select the compression backend.
Only one backend should be enabled at a time, or else one will see an unstable order which is currently
`zlib-ng`, `zlib-rs`, `cloudflare_zlib`, `miniz_oxide` and which may change at any time.

-
`rust_backend`*(enabled by default)*— Use the pure Rust`miniz_oxide`backend (default). This implementation uses only safe Rust code and doesn’t require a C compiler. It provides good performance for most use cases while being completely portable.Note that this feature at some point may be switched to use `zlib-rs`instead.
-
`zlib-rs``unsafe`code. It does not require a C compiler but uses`unsafe`Rust for optimization.
-
`miniz_oxide`*(enabled by default)*— Use the pure Rust`miniz_oxide`backend.
-
`zlib`
-
`zlib-default``zlib`but enables additional features from libz-sys.
-
`zlib-ng-compat``zlib-ng`feature. When using this feature, if any crate in your dependency graph explicitly requests stock zlib, or uses libz-sys directly without`default-features = false`, you’ll get stock zlib rather than zlib-ng. See[the libz-sys README](https://github.com/rust-lang/libz-sys/blob/main/README.md)for details. To avoid that, use the`"zlib-ng"`feature instead.
-
`zlib-ng`
-
`cloudflare_zlib`- ⚠ Does not support 32-bit CPUs and is incompatible with mingw.
- ⚠ May cause conflicts if other crates use different zlib versions.

-
`miniz-sys``rust_backend`, provided for backwards compatibility. Use`rust_backend`instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#internal-features)Internal Features

These features are used internally for backend selection and should not be enabled directly by users. They are documented here to aid with maintenance.

- `any_zlib`- **Internal:**Marker feature indicating that any zlib-based C backend is enabled. This is automatically enabled by- `zlib-rs`,- `zlib`,- `zlib-ng`,- `zlib-ng-compat`, and- `cloudflare_zlib`. Do not enable this feature directly; instead, choose a specific backend feature.
- `any_c_zlib`- **Internal:**Marker feature indicating that any C based fully zlib compatible backend is enabled. This is automatically enabled by- `zlib`,- `zlib-ng`,- `zlib-ng-compat`, and- `cloudflare_zlib`. Do not enable this feature directly; instead, choose a specific backend feature.
- `any_impl`- *(enabled by default)*—- **Internal:**Marker feature indicating that any compression backend is enabled. This is automatically enabled by all backend features to ensure at least one implementation is available. Do not enable this feature directly; instead, choose a specific backend feature.

[§](https://docs.rs#ambiguous-feature-selection)Ambiguous feature selection

As Cargo features are additive, while backends are not, there is an order in which backends become active if multiple are selected.

- zlib-ng
- zlib-rs
- cloudflare_zlib
- miniz_oxide

[§](https://docs.rs#organization)Organization

This crate consists of three main modules: `bufread`, `read`, and `write`. Each module
implements DEFLATE, zlib, and gzip for [ std::io::BufRead](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.BufRead.html) input types,

[input types, and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Read.html)

`std::io::Read`[output types respectively.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html)

`std::io::Write`Use the [ bufread](https://docs.rs/bufread/index.html) implementations if you can provide a

`BufRead` type for the input.
The `&[u8]` slice type implements the `BufRead` trait.The [ read](https://docs.rs/read/index.html) implementations conveniently wrap a

`Read` type in a `BufRead` implementation.
However, the `read` implementations may
[read past the end of the input data](https://github.com/rust-lang/flate2-rs/issues/338), making the

`Read` type useless for subsequent reads of the input. If you need to re-use the
`Read` type, wrap it in a [, use the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/buffered/bufreader/struct.BufReader.html)

`std::io::BufReader``bufread` implementations,
and perform subsequent reads on the `BufReader`.The [ write](https://docs.rs/write/index.html) implementations are most useful when there is no way to create a

`BufRead`
type, notably when reading async iterators (streams).```
use futures::{Stream, StreamExt};
use std::io::{Result, Write as _};
async fn decompress_gzip_stream<S, I>(stream: S) -> Result<Vec<u8>>
where
    S: Stream<Item = I>,
    I: AsRef<[u8]>
{
    let mut stream = std::pin::pin!(stream);
    let mut w = Vec::<u8>::new();
    let mut decoder = flate2::write::GzDecoder::new(w);
    while let Some(input) = stream.next().await {
        decoder.write_all(input.as_ref())?;
    }
    decoder.finish()
}
```
Note that types which operate over a specific trait often implement the mirroring trait as well.
For example a `bufread::DeflateDecoder<T>` *also* implements the
[ Write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html) trait if

`T: Write`. That is, the “dual trait” is forwarded directly
to the underlying object if available.[§](https://docs.rs#about-multi-member-gzip-files)About multi-member Gzip files

While most `gzip` files one encounters will have a single *member* that can be read
with the [ GzDecoder](https://docs.rs/bufread/struct.GzDecoder.html), there may be some files which have multiple members.

A [ GzDecoder](https://docs.rs/bufread/struct.GzDecoder.html) will only read the first member of gzip data, which may unexpectedly
provide partial results when a multi-member gzip file is encountered.

`GzDecoder` is appropriate
for data that is designed to be read as single members from a multi-member file. `bufread::GzDecoder`
and `write::GzDecoder` also allow non-gzip data following gzip data to be handled.The [ MultiGzDecoder](https://docs.rs/bufread/struct.MultiGzDecoder.html) on the other hand will decode all members of a

`gzip` file
into one consecutive stream of bytes, which hides the underlying *members*entirely. If a file contains non-gzip data after the gzip data, MultiGzDecoder will emit an error after decoding the gzip data. This behavior matches the

`gzip`,
`gunzip`, and `zcat` command line tools.## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [bufread](https://docs.rs/bufread/index.html)
- Types which operate over `BufRead`
- [read](https://docs.rs/read/index.html)
- Types which operate over `Read`
- [write](https://docs.rs/write/index.html)
- Types which operate over `Write`
